label: Mission statement
body:
Effect Index serves as the platform for the [Subjective Effect Index (SEI)](/effects), a resource containing formalised documentation of the vast number of distinct subjective states that may occur under the influence of hallucinogens. We strive to comprehensively document and describe the wide variety of potential hallucinogenic experiences. The SEI is presented in an easily readable format that contains not only descriptions, but also image, video, and audio [replications](/replications) of these effects.

We believe that in pioneering formalised subjective effect documentation, we may demystify the psychedelic experience. This has the potential to allow hallucinogen usage to become more culturally acceptable, better understood, and create a platform on top of which these substances may be more easily studied.

Effect Index was initially founded as a side project on 30 June, 2017 by [Josie Kins](/contributors/josie), the founder of [PsychonautWiki](https://psychonautwiki.org) and [DisregardEverythingISay](https://disregardeverythingisay.com/). It serves as a platform for content that has been in constant development for the previous six years on these sites. However, the aforementioned content is now hosted on its own dedicated platform with the hope of further spreading the documentation and creating a universal terminology set that gives people the vernacular to fully describe experiences that were previously considered ineffable.

If you find this project interesting, we encourage you to join our active communities within both our [subreddit](https://reddit.com/r/replications) and our [Discord](/discord).

label: Homepage intro, lead paragraph
body: **Effect Index,** is a resource dedicated to establishing the field of formalised subjective effect documentation. It is the home of the [Subjective Effect Index](/effects) (SEI), which contains {{effectCount}} effect descriptions that exist to serve as a comprehensive map of all potential experiences that can occur under the influence of any class of psychoactive compound, particularly hallucinogens.

label: Homepage intro, method paragraph
body: The effects identified here are accompanied by detailed descriptions of how it feels to experience them. These are written in an objective and [consistent writing style](/documentation-style-guide) based upon phenomenological observation and avoids the use of metaphor or analogy. The descriptions also strive to use language that is as simple and understandable as possible. This has been done with the hope that they will serve as a universal terminology that allows people to describe and discuss that which was previously considered ineffable.

label: Homepage intro, organisation paragraph
body: These effects are organised into categories based on the sense affected and their behaviour. Many of these are further broken down into levels, subcomponents, and variations in style, which can occur across different substances. Detailed [replications](/replications) are included whenever possible to supplement the text descriptions in the form of images, audio clips, and animations.

label: Psychedelic definition
body: **Psychedelics** (also known as serotonergic hallucinogens) are a subclass of hallucinogen that change perception, emotion, and thought. The user usually stays aware that a drug is causing the experience. Psychedelics act mainly on a serotonin receptor called 5-HT2A, which loosens the normal filtering of incoming information in the brain. Common effects are stronger color, flowing geometric patterns, deeper emotion, and a sense of insight. The term dates from 1956. It comes from the Greek *psyche* ("mind") and *delos* ("to reveal"), and means "mind-manifesting."

label: Dissociative definition
body: **Dissociatives** are a subclass of hallucinogen that produce a feeling of detachment from the body, the sense of self, and the surroundings. Dissociatives mainly block NMDA receptors, which are part of the glutamate system. This system binds sensory information and the sense of self into one coherent experience. The block interrupts this system and creates the sense of disconnection. At low doses, the effect is a floaty, dreamlike state. At high doses, the effect is a full out-of-body experience.

label: Entactogen definition
body: **Entactogens** (also known as empathogens) are a class of psychoactive substances that produce emotional openness, empathy, warmth, and closeness to other people. Entactogens mainly cause a large release of serotonin, with some dopamine and noradrenaline. This mix makes the experience mildly euphoric and social, not strongly hallucinatory. The name comes from the Greek *en* ("within"), the Latin *tactus* ("touch"), and *-gen* ("to produce"). Together these parts mean "to touch within."

label: Stimulant definition
body: **Stimulants** (also known as "uppers") are a class of psychoactive substances that speed up the central nervous system. They increase energy, alertness, wakefulness, and focus. They also reduce appetite and fatigue. Stimulants mainly raise the levels of dopamine and noradrenaline, the drive and alertness chemicals of the brain. These raised levels are also the reason that a crash often follows the effects. The name comes from the Latin *stimulare*, which means "to goad on."

label: Nootropic definition
body: **Nootropics** (also known as cognitive enhancers or "smart drugs") are a class of psychoactive substances that support mental performance, such as memory, focus, learning, and motivation. They usually have few side effects. Nootropics do not share one mechanism: some change neurotransmitter levels, some increase blood flow to the brain, and some protect brain cells. Their effects are therefore small and gradual, and they do not produce an obvious high. The term dates from 1972 and comes from the Greek *noos* ("mind") and *tropein* ("to turn"), which mean "mind-turning."

label: Antidepressant definition
body: **Antidepressants** are a class of psychoactive medications that treat depression and related conditions. Most antidepressants slow the reabsorption of serotonin or noradrenaline in the brain, which keeps more of it active over time. For this reason, they have no immediate effect and take weeks to work. An antidepressant is not the opposite of a "depressant" drug. The two words use "depress" in different senses: one refers to the mood disorder, and the other refers to a slower nervous system.

label: Antipsychotic definition
body: **Antipsychotics** (also known as neuroleptics) are a class of psychoactive medications that manage psychosis. Psychosis includes hallucinations, delusions, and disordered thought. Antipsychotics mainly block dopamine receptors. This block reduces dopamine signaling, which is too high during a psychotic state.

label: Opioid definition
body: **Opioids** are a class of psychoactive substances that relieve pain and produce euphoria, relaxation, and contentment. They also cause sedation. At high doses, opioids slow breathing to a dangerous degree. Opioids imitate endorphins, the natural painkilling chemicals of the body, and act on the same opioid receptors. The name comes from *opium*, the extract of the poppy, and *-oid* ("resembling"). The term "opiate" covers only natural poppy derivatives, but "opioid" covers any substance that acts on these receptors.

label: Deliriant definition
body: **Deliriants** are a subclass of hallucinogen that produce delirium: a state of confusion, an inability to tell hallucinations from reality, and frequent amnesia afterward. Deliriants block acetylcholine, a neurotransmitter that the brain needs for memory, attention, and a stable view of the real world. Psychedelics and dissociatives usually cause hallucinations that the user knows are unreal. Deliriants instead produce "true" hallucinations, which the user cannot tell apart from reality. The name comes from the Latin *delirare*, which means "to go off the track."

label: Sedative-hypnotics definition
body: **Sedative-hypnotics** are psychoactive substances that usually cause sedation, drowsiness, or sleep. This class holds several families of depressant drugs with different mechanisms: benzodiazepines, barbiturates, alcohol, GABA analogs, and some substances that act on voltage-gated calcium channels. Opioids have their own category.

label: Cannabinoid definition
body: **Cannabinoids** are a class of psychoactive substances that change mood, appetite, memory, perception, and pain through the endocannabinoid system of the body. They act on the CB1 receptors that the body's own cannabis-like signal chemicals normally use. Common effects are relaxation, a changed sense of time, and more appetite. The name comes from the *Cannabis* plant, where these compounds were first identified.

label: Hallucinogens (umbrella tab) definition
body: **Hallucinogens** are a class of psychoactive substances that produce strong changes in perception, mood, and thought. The experience often feels like a different state of consciousness, not a stronger or weaker version of normal awareness. There are three subclasses of hallucinogens: psychedelics, dissociatives, and deliriants. Each subclass acts on a different brain system and produces a different type of experience. The name comes from the Latin *hallucinari*, which means "to wander in the mind."

label: Depressants (umbrella tab) definition
body: **Depressants** (also known as "downers") are a class of psychoactive substances that slow the central nervous system. They produce relaxation, calm, less anxiety, drowsiness, and lower inhibition. Most depressants strengthen GABA, the main inhibitory or "braking" system of the brain. The word "depressant" means lower nervous-system activity. It does not mean sadness.

label: SEI intro, lead paragraph
body: The **Subjective Effect Index** is a comprehensive catalogue of {{effectCount}} subjective effects that may occur under the influence of psychoactive substances.

label: SEI intro, writing-style paragraph
body: The effects are accompanied by detailed descriptions written in a consistent style that avoids flowery metaphors, using simple and accessible language to serve as a universal terminology for communicating experiences that are difficult to convey.

label: SEI intro, organisation paragraph
body: Effects are organised into categories based on the senses they affect and their behavior, with many broken down into leveling systems, subcomponents, and style variations. Image, video, and audio replications supplement text-based descriptions.

label: Sensory tab intro
body: Sensory effects are subjective effects that directly alter a person's senses. These can include any combination of sight, sound, touch, taste, and smell.

label: Cognitive tab intro
body: Cognitive effects are subjective effects that directly alter or introduce new content to an element of a person's cognition.

label: Physical tab intro
body: Physical effects are subjective effects that directly affect part of a person's physical body.

label: Visual Effects description
body: Visual effects are defined as any subjective effect that directly alters a person's sense of sight.

label: Visual Amplifications description
body: Visual amplifications are defined as any subjective effect that increases, enhances, accelerates, or intensifies a facet of a person's sense of sight.

label: Visual Suppressions description
body: Visual suppressions are defined as any subjective effect that decreases a person's ability to perceive the external environment through their sense of sight.

label: Visual Distortions description
body: Visual distortions are defined as any subjective effect that alters the perception or appearance of pre-existing visual data without adding any entirely new content.

label: Geometric Patterns description
body: Geometric patterns are defined as any subjective effect that introduces complex arrays of shapes, colours, symbols, patterns, geometry, form constants, and fractals to one's field of vision.

label: Hallucinatory Effects description
body: Hallucinatory states are defined as any subjective effect that changes the perception or appearance of pre-existing sensory data by adding entirely new content in a manner similar to that of dreams.

label: Auditory Effects description
body: Effects that directly alter a person's sense of hearing.

label: Smell & Taste Effects description
body: Smell and taste effects are defined as any subjective effect that directly alters either a person's sense of smell or taste.

label: Tactile Effects description
body: Tactile effects are defined as any subjective effect that directly alters a person's sense of touch.

label: Multisensory Effects description
body: Multisensory effects are defined as any subjective effect that directly alters two or more senses at a time.

label: Disconnective Effects description
body: Disconnective effects are defined as any subjective effect that feels as if it disconnects one from the external environment, their senses, and/or their consciousness.

label: Cognitive Effects description
body: Cognitive effects are subjective effects that directly alter or introduce new content to an element of a person's cognition.

label: Cognitive Amplifications description
body: Cognitive amplifications are defined as any subjective effect that increases, enhances, accelerates, or intensifies a facet of a person's cognition.

label: Cognitive Suppressions description
body: Cognitive suppressions are defined as any subjective effect that decreases the intensity of a facet of a person's cognition.

label: Novel Cognitive States description
body: Novel cognitive states are defined as any cognitive effect that does not merely amplify or suppress familiar states of mind; rather, it induces an experience that is qualitatively different from that of ordinary consciousness.

label: Psychological States description
body: Psychological states are defined as any cognitive effect that is either established within the psychological literature or arises as a result of the complex interplay between more simplistic components such as cognitive enhancements and suppressions.

label: Transpersonal States description
body: Transpersonal states are defined as any subjective effect that feels as if it alters a person's cognition in a manner that relates to their place in the universe, the inner workings of reality or consciousness, and/or the context of their existence. The highest manifestations of these effects fall under what are commonly known as 'peak', 'transcendent' or 'transformative' experiences.

label: Transpersonal Effects description
body:
Transpersonal effects are defined as any subjective effect that feels as if it alters a person's cognition in a manner that relates to their place in the universe, the inner workings of reality or consciousness, and/or the context of their existence. The highest manifestations of these effects fall under what are commonly known as "peak", "transcendent" or "transformative" experiences.

These effects are typically associated with high dose psychedelic or dissociative experiences. They can occur regardless of the person's spiritual or religious beliefs and often have a distinct and lasting impact on the user's perspective of the world around them. During the experience of a substance-induced transpersonal state, the information conveyed is often felt to be a real and objective truth. However, the person will often come to disagree with these supposed "epiphanies" once the effects of the substance have worn off.

It should be noted that these mind-states are the least reproducible of all effects within the Subjective Effect Index. Simply taking more of a given substance does not necessarily increase the chances of having these states occur. Instead, they seem to rely more on contextual factors, such as the person's set and setting.

This page lists the various transpersonal effects that can occur under the influence of certain psychoactive compounds.

label: Physical Effects description
body: Physical effects are subjective effects that directly alter a person's perception of their physical body or its physiological functions.

label: Physical Amplifications description
body: Physical amplifications are defined as any subjective effect that increases, enhances, accelerates, or intensifies a facet of a person's physical body.

label: Physical Suppressions description
body: Physical suppressions are defined as any subjective effect that decreases or reduces a facet of a person's physical body.

label: Physical Alterations description
body: Physical alterations are defined as any subjective effect that changes a facet of a person's physical body in a manner which is not uncomfortable and does not involve a clearly definable enhancement or suppression.

label: Uncomfortable Physical Effects description
body: Uncomfortable physical effects are defined as any substance-induced alteration of a person's physical state that is unpleasant, undesirable, painful, or otherwise a source of distress.

label: Cardiovascular Effects description
body: Cardiovascular effects are defined as any uncomfortable physical effect that relates to the heart and blood vessels.

label: Neurological Effects description
body: Neurological effects are defined as any uncomfortable physical effect that relates to the brain and its blood vessels.

label: Uncomfortable Bodily Effects description
body: Uncomfortable bodily effects are defined as any uncomfortable physical effect that relates to the overall body and cannot be categorized as cardiovascular or cerebrovascular.

label: Fair-use & takedown notice
body:
**Why this art is here.** We host replications for educational and archival purposes: they show what altered states of consciousness actually look and sound like, so you can understand these experiences without having them. We believe this non-commercial, educational use constitutes fair use. We have tried in good faith to credit every artist and to link their pages so you can find and support them. Rights remain with the original creator or rightsholder unless an individual item states another license. See the [licensing terms](/docs/license#replication-media-terms).

If your art appears here and you want it taken down, email [contact@dose.wiki](mailto:contact@dose.wiki) and we will remove it. Use the same address to correct a misattribution, ask a question, or share more of your work.

Any contribution is greatly appreciated!

label: Discord intro
body:
The official Effect Index community is hosted on Discord and may be joined [here.]({{discordInvite}})

This a semi-private community and is not primarily for general conversation; instead, it aims to be a place of discussion and co-operation for progressing the field of formalised subjective effect documentation. For this reason, we tend to only invite people who genuinely want to contribute to the project. This can include anyone from proofreaders, trip reporters, web developers, programmers, replicators, artists, and more.

If you have an interest in contributing to and taking part in our community's various projects, please contact us within the public waiting room channel and tell us why you are interested in this project. Thanks!

label: Discord rules
items: You must be at least 18+ years old.
You may not discuss any drug sources. Not even in DMs.
Keep specific topics within their relevant channels.
This community is inclusive and does not accept any kind of racism, homophobia, sexism, transphobia, ableism, general hatefulness, etc, etc.
This community is relatively Safe For Work (SFW), please do not post overtly sexual or edgy content. This includes hornyposting and excessive shitposting.
